claim: The animacy organization in ventral temporal cortex (VTC) reflects a continuum rather than a dichotomy.
source: The principles underlying the animacy organization of the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) remain hotly debated, with recent evidence pointing to an animacy continuum rather than a dichotomy.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Connolly et al., 2012; Sha et al., 2015) and replicated in the current study's results.

claim: Animate and inanimate objects form distinct representational clusters in ventral temporal cortex.
source: These categories form distinct representational clusters (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008) and activate anatomically distinct regions of VTC (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014; Chao et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Visual categorizability and agency explain independent components of the animacy continuum in VTC.
source: Using fMRI, we found that visual categorizability and agency explained independent components of the animacy continuum in VTC.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis showing independent correlations after regression.

claim: Visual categorizability and agency together fully explain the animacy continuum in VTC.
source: Modeled together, they fully explained the animacy continuum.
evidence: Supported by combined model reaching noise ceiling in fMRI data analysis.

claim: Clusters explained by visual categorizability are localized posterior to clusters explained by agency in VTC.
source: Finally, clusters explained by visual categorizability were localized posterior to clusters explained by agency.
evidence: Supported by searchlight analysis showing anatomical separation.

claim: The correlation between thoughtfulness and feelings ratings was at the noise ceiling of both ratings (τ = 0.70).
source: The correlation between the thoughtfulness and feelings ratings (τ = 0.70) was at the noise ceiling of both those ratings (τthought = 0.69, τfeel = 0.70).
evidence: Supported by behavioral rating data from N=16 participants.

claim: Agency was measured as the average of thoughtfulness and feelings ratings.
source: We therefore averaged the thoughtfulness and feelings ratings and considered the averaged rating a measure of agency.
evidence: Based on high correlation between thoughtfulness and feelings ratings.

claim: Image categorizability and perceptual categorizability were positively correlated for the 12 selected animals (Kendall's τ = 0.64).
source: The two measures of visual categorizability were positively correlated for the 12 animals that were selected for the fMRI experiment (Kendall's τ = 0.64), indicating that they partly reflect similar animate-selective visual properties of the objects.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between CNN-based and behavioral measures.

claim: The final set of 12 animals had low correlations between image categorizability, agency, and familiarity (τ < 0.13).
source: This was successful, as indicated by low correlations between these variables (τ < 0.13, for all correlations).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of the selected stimulus set.

claim: The mean cross-validated training accuracy of animate-inanimate classification in VTC was 89.6%.
source: The mean cross-validated training accuracy (animacy localizer) of animate-inanimate classification in VTC was 89.6%, while the cross-experiment accuracy in classifying the 16 stimuli from the main fMRI experiment was 71.3%, indicating reliable animacy information in both experiments.
evidence: Supported by SVM classification analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Among the animals, humans were the most animate whereas reptiles and insects were the least animate.
source: Among the animals, humans were the most animate whereas reptiles and insects were the least animate (they were classified as inanimate, on average).
evidence: Supported by animacy scores from fMRI classification analysis.

claim: VTC animacy scores correlated positively with image categorizability (τ = 0.16; p = 10-3).
source: VTC animacy scores correlated positively with all three measures: image categorizability (τ = 0.16; p = 10-3), perceptual categorizability (τ = 0.26; p < 10-4); and agency (τ = 0.30; p < 10-4).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of fMRI data with behavioral measures.

claim: VTC animacy scores correlated positively with perceptual categorizability (τ = 0.26; p < 10-4).
source: VTC animacy scores correlated positively with all three measures: image categorizability (τ = 0.16; p = 10-3), perceptual categorizability (τ = 0.26; p < 10-4); and agency (τ = 0.30; p < 10-4).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of fMRI data with behavioral measures.

claim: VTC animacy scores correlated positively with agency (τ = 0.30; p < 10-4).
source: VTC animacy scores correlated positively with all three measures: image categorizability (τ = 0.16; p = 10-3), perceptual categorizability (τ = 0.26; p < 10-4); and agency (τ = 0.30; p < 10-4).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of fMRI data with behavioral measures.

claim: The correlation between VTC animacy and agency remained positive (τ = 0.23; p < 10-4) after regressing out image categorizability and perceptual categorizability.
source: The correlation between VTC animacy and agency remained positive in all individual participants (τ = 0.23; p < 10-4 Figure 4D) after regressing out both image categorizability and perceptual categorizability.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The correlation between VTC animacy and visual categorizability remained positive (τ = 0.12; p = 4.7 × 103) after regressing out agency.
source: Similarly, the correlation between VTC animacy and visual categorizability remained positive after regressing out agency (τ = 0.12; p = 4.7 × 103).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The combined model of visual categorizability and agency had a higher correlation with VTC animacy than any of the three factors alone.
source: The resultant combined model (derived separately for each left-out participant) had a higher correlation with VTC animacy than any of the three factors alone (within-participant comparisons - ΔIC = 0.21, p < 10-4; ΔPC = 0.10, p = 6 x 10-4, ΔAg = 0.07, p = 8.3 x 10-3).
evidence: Supported by leave-one-out regression analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The correlation between the combined model and VTC animacy (τ = 0.37) is at VTC animacy noise ceiling (τNC = 0.39).
source: Furthermore, the correlation between the combined model and VTC animacy (τ = 0.37; Figure 4D) is at VTC animacy noise ceiling (τNC = 0.39; Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by comparison of combined model correlation to noise ceiling.

claim: The independent visual categorizability contribution was located in posterior VTC (LH: 1584 mm3, center MNI coordinates: x = -38, y = -80, z = 7; RH: 7184 mm3, center coordinates: x = 41, y = -71, z = 1).
source: Moreover, there was a consistent anatomical mapping of the two factors: the independent visual categorizability contribution (LH: 1584 mm3, center Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) coordinates: x = -38, y = -80, z = 7; RH: 7184 mm3, center coordinates: x = 41, y = -71, z = 1) was located posterior to the independent agency contribution (LH: 592 mm3, center coordinates: x = -42, y = -56, z = -19; RH: 4000 mm3, center coordinates: x = 39, y = -52, z = -12), extending from VTC into the lateral occipital regions.
evidence: Supported by searchlight analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The independent agency contribution was located in anterior VTC (LH: 592 mm3, center coordinates: x = -42, y = -56, z = -19; RH: 4000 mm3, center coordinates: x = 39, y = -52, z = -12).
source: Moreover, there was a consistent anatomical mapping of the two factors: the independent visual categorizability contribution (LH: 1584 mm3, center Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) coordinates: x = -38, y = -80, z = 7; RH: 7184 mm3, center coordinates: x = 41, y = -71, z = 1) was located posterior to the independent agency contribution (LH: 592 mm3, center coordinates: x = -42, y = -56, z = -19; RH: 4000 mm3, center coordinates: x = 39, y = -52, z = -12), extending from VTC into the lateral occipital regions.
evidence: Supported by searchlight analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The posterior-anterior organization of visual categorizability and agency was observed in both hemispheres, though stronger in the right hemisphere.
source: A similar posterior-anterior organization was observed in both hemispheres (Figure 5B), though stronger in the right hemisphere.
evidence: Supported by searchlight analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: According to the visual categorization hypothesis, the animacy organization supports efficient readout of superordinate category information for rapid visual categorization.
source: According to the visual categorization hypothesis, this animate-inanimate organization supports the efficient readout of superordinate category information, allowing for the rapid visual categorization of objects as being animate or inanimate (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical framework.

claim: The ability to rapidly detect animals may have constituted an evolutionary advantage.
source: The ability to rapidly detect animals may have constituted an evolutionary advantage (Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; New et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to evolutionary psychology literature.

claim: According to the agency hypothesis, the animacy organization reflects the degree to which animals share psychological characteristics with humans.
source: According to this agency hypothesis, the animacy organization reflects the degree to which animals share psychological characteristics with humans, such as the ability to perform goal-directed actions and experiencing thoughts and feelings.
evidence: Supported by theoretical framework and citations to previous work on agency.

claim: VTC shows animate-like responses to simple shapes whose movements imply agency.
source: This continuum was interpreted as evidence that VTC reflects the psychological property of animacy, or agency, in line with earlier work showing animate-like VTC responses to simple shapes whose movements imply agency (Castelli et al., 2002; Martin and Weisberg, 2003; Gobbini et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Visual categorizability of animals correlates with the representational distance from the decision boundary of an animate-inanimate classifier trained on VTC activity patterns.
source: Indeed, recent work showed that the visual categorizability of animals (as measured by reaction times) correlates with the representational distance of those animals from the decision boundary of an animate-inanimate classifier trained on VTC activity patterns (Carlson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Animals' visual categorizability and agency are correlated.
source: The difficulty in distinguishing between the visual categorization and agency hypotheses lies in the fact that animals' visual categorizability and agency are correlated.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the properties of animals.

claim: Four-legged mammals are relatively fast to categorize as animate and are also judged to be psychologically relatively similar to humans.
source: For example, four-legged mammals are relatively fast to categorize as animate and are also judged to be psychologically relatively similar to humans.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about animal perception.

claim: The CNN VGG-16 contains 13 convolutional layers and 3 fully-connected layers.
source: A schematic of the convolutional neural network (CNN) VGG-16 is shown. The CNN contains 13 convolutional layers (shown in green), which are constrained to perform the spatially-local computations across the visual field, and three fully-connected layers (shown in blue).
evidence: Supported by description and Figure 1B showing CNN architecture.

claim: The average cross-validation accuracy of the CNN animate-inanimate classifier was 92.2%.
source: The average cross-validation accuracy was 92.2%.
evidence: Supported by CNN classification analysis.

claim: 29 healthy adults participated in the visual search task, of which 21 were selected for analysis.
source: 29 healthy adults participated in this experiment, of which 21 (9 females; age range: 19–62, median: 27) were selected according to the conditions specified below to obtain an estimate of perceptual categorizability.
evidence: Supported by description of participant selection.

claim: All participants in the visual search task had accuracies of 90% and higher in every block.
source: All participants had accuracies of 90% and higher in every block.
evidence: Supported by behavioral task performance data.

claim: For the 21 selected participants in the visual search task, the mean training accuracy was 63.4% (>50%, p < 10-4).
source: For the relevant 21 participants, the mean training accuracy was 63.4% (>50%, p < 10-4), and the mean test accuracy was 70.0% (>50%, p < 10-4).
evidence: Supported by SVM classification analysis of behavioral data.

claim: For the 21 selected participants in the visual search task, the mean test accuracy was 70.0% (>50%, p < 10-4).
source: For the relevant 21 participants, the mean training accuracy was 63.4% (>50%, p < 10-4), and the mean test accuracy was 70.0% (>50%, p < 10-4).
evidence: Supported by SVM classification analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Sixteen healthy adults participated in the ratings experiment.
source: Sixteen healthy adults participated in this experiment (9 females; all students at the University of Trento).
evidence: Supported by description of participant sample.

claim: Seventeen healthy adults participated in the fMRI experiment.
source: Seventeen healthy adults (6 females; age range: 20 − 32, median: 25) were scanned at the Center for Mind/Brain Sciences of the University of Trento.
evidence: Supported by description of participant sample.

claim: The main fMRI experiment consisted of eight runs.
source: The main experiment consisted of eight runs.
evidence: Supported by description of experimental design.

claim: Each run in the main fMRI experiment consisted of 80 trials composed of 64 object trials and 16 fixation-only trials.
source: Each run consisted of 80 trials that were composed of 64 object trials and 16 fixation-only trials.
evidence: Supported by description of experimental design.

claim: The animacy localizer experiment included 36 animate and 36 inanimate stimuli.
source: During the localizer, participants viewed grey-scale images of 36 animate and 36 inanimate stimuli in a block design.
evidence: Supported by description of experimental design.

claim: VTC was defined to extend from −71 to −21 on the y-axis of the MNI coordinates.
source: The region extended from −71 to −21 on the y-axis of the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) coordinates.
evidence: Supported by description of ROI definition.

claim: The animacy organization in VTC is not fully explained by visual categorization demands.
source: The current results contribute to these findings by showing that (part of) the animacy continuum reflects the perceived agency of the animals: animals that were perceived as being relatively more capable of having thoughts and feelings were more easily classified as animate in VTC. This correlation persisted when regressing out the influence of animal-diagnostic visual features. These findings provide evidence that the animacy continuum is not fully explained by visual categorization demands, with perceived agency contributing significantly to the animacy organization.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data showing independent agency contribution.

claim: Regions in visual cortex responsive to social stimuli are functionally connected to the precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Regions in visual cortex responsive to social stimuli are functionally connected to the precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex – regions involved in social perspective taking and reasoning about mental states (Simmons and Martin, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous connectivity study.

claim: Category-selective responses in visual cortex are integral parts of large-scale domain-selective networks.
source: Indeed, it is increasingly appreciated that category-selective responses in visual cortex are not solely driven by bottom-up visual input but are integral parts of large-scale domain-selective networks involved in domain-specific tasks like social cognition, tool use, navigation, or reading (Peelen and Downing, 2017; Price and Devlin, 2011; Martin, 2007; Mahon and Caramazza, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical literature.

claim: The posterior-anterior organization of visual categorizability and agency mirrors the hierarchical organization of visual cortex.
source: The unique contributions of agency and visual categorizability were observed in different parts of VTC, with the agency cluster located anterior to the visual categorizability cluster. This posterior-anterior organization mirrors the well-known hierarchical organization of visual cortex.
evidence: Based on comparison to known hierarchical organization and current findings.

claim: A similar posterior-anterior difference was observed in studies dissociating shape and category representations in VTC.
source: A similar posterior-anterior difference was observed in studies dissociating shape and category representations in VTC, with object shape represented posterior to object category (Proklova et al., 2016; Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Animate-selective responses in VTC are observed for shape- and texture-matched objects.
source: For example, animate-selective responses in VTC are also observed for shape- and texture-matched objects (Proklova et al., 2016; Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016) and animate-like VTC responses can be evoked by geometric shapes that, through their movement, imply the presence of social agents (Castelli et al., 2002; Martin and Weisberg, 2003; Gobbini et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Mid-level perceptual features allow for distinguishing between animate and inanimate objects.
source: Furthermore, recent work has shown that mid-level perceptual features allow for distinguishing between animate and inanimate objects (Levin et al., 2001; Long et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2017; Zachariou et al., 2018) and that these features can elicit a VTC animacy organization in the absence of object recognition (Long et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on perceptual features.

claim: The VGG-16 CNN was pre-trained on images from the ImageNet ILSVRC classification challenge.
source: The CNN was taken from the MatConvNet package (Vedaldi and Lenc, 2015) and was pre-trained on images from the ImageNet ILSVRC classification challenge (Russakovsky et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by description of CNN training procedure.

claim: Activations were extracted from 960 colored images, of which 480 contain an animal or animal parts and the rest contain inanimate objects or their parts.
source: Activations were extracted from the final fully-connected layer, prior to the softmax operation, for 960 colored images obtained from Kiani et al. (2007) of which 480 contain an animal or animal parts and the rest contain inanimate objects or their parts.
evidence: Supported by description of CNN training data.

claim: The dimensionality of CNN activations was reduced to 495 dimensions using principal component analysis.
source: The dimensionality of the activations was reduced to 495 dimensions using principal component analysis in order to reduce the training time while keeping the captured variance high (more details can be found in Thorat, 2017).
evidence: Supported by description of data preprocessing.

claim: Imaging data were acquired using a MedSpec 4-T head scanner equipped with an eight-channel head coil.
source: Imaging data were acquired using a MedSpec 4-T head scanner (Bruker Biospin GmbH, Rheinstetten, Germany), equipped with an eight-channel head coil.
evidence: Supported by description of MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional images were collected with T2*-weighted EPIs (repetition time = 2.0s, echo-time = 33 ms, 73° flip-angle, 3 mm × 3 mm × 3 mm voxel size).
source: For functional imaging, T2*-weighted EPIs were collected (repetition time = 2.0s, echo-time = 33 ms, 73° flip-angle, 3 mm × 3 mm × 3 mm voxel size, 1 mm gap, 34 slices, 192 mm field of view, 64 × 64 matrix size).
evidence: Supported by description of MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: No spatial smoothing was applied to the fMRI data.
source: No spatial smoothing was applied.
evidence: Supported by description of preprocessing steps.

claim: The searchlight spheres contained 100 proximal voxels.
source: In the whole-brain searchlight analysis, the searchlight spheres contained 100 proximal voxels.
evidence: Supported by description of searchlight analysis parameters.

claim: Threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) with a permutation test was used to correct for multiple comparisons.
source: Threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE; Smith and Nichols, 2009) with a permutation test was used to correct for multiple comparisons of the accuracies relative to baseline (50%).
evidence: Supported by description of statistical correction method.

claim: Bootstrap analysis with 10,000 samples was used for hypothesis testing.
source: Hypothesis testing was done with bootstrap analysis. We sampled 10,000 times with replacement from the observations being tested.
evidence: Supported by description of statistical methods.
